title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the road, the family and the words

questions.prompt: Kingston is the narrator's son, and Samantha is Kingston's wife. What is Samantha to the narrator?

options.text: her daughter-in-law
her eldest granddaughter
her own mother-in-law
her sister-in-law

questions.explanation: "her daughter-in-law" is right: the wife of your son is your daughter-in-law, and the narrator is Samantha's mother-in-law in return. "her own mother-in-law" reverses the two women. "her sister-in-law" would be the wife of a brother, and "her eldest granddaughter" would be the daughter of her own child, one generation further down.

questions.prompt: Almost every verb of this text is in the simple past. What does that tell a reader about the text itself?

options.text: It describes an ordinary daily routine.
It gives instructions to a young driver.
It narrates a series of past events.
It predicts what will happen next.

questions.explanation: "It narrates a series of past events." is right: the simple past is the tense of the finished event, so a text built on it lines events up one after the other. "It describes an ordinary daily routine." would call for the present simple, "It predicts what will happen next." for will, and "It gives instructions to a young driver." for imperatives. The tense of a text and its function always travel together.

questions.prompt: Put these three moments of the story in the order in which they happen: (1) the telephone rings inside her car; (2) the other car brakes and settles behind her; (3) she kisses her husband goodnight at the centre.
questions.explanation: "3, 2, 1" is the order: the visit comes first, since she is driving home from it; the strange car appears on the road; and the telephone rings last, when the fear is at its highest. "1, 2, 3" reads the three numbers as they are printed instead of following the story. "2, 3, 1" and "3, 1, 2" both put the telephone before the car that follows her, so the frightening drive would have no cause left.

questions.prompt: The narrator telephones her son and Samantha answers: "He isn't home." Which fact does that reply add to the story?

options.text: Kingston had left his wife a few weeks before that.
Kingston was out of the house at that moment.
Samantha did not want to speak to the narrator.
Donald had come back from the centre that evening.

questions.explanation: "Kingston was out of the house at that moment." is exactly what the three words say, no more: he is not there when his mother calls. "Kingston had left his wife a few weeks before that." turns an absence of one evening into a separation. "Samantha did not want to speak to the narrator." contradicts the fact that she picks the telephone up, and "Donald had come back from the centre that evening." is impossible, since the narrator has just left him there.

questions.prompt: Which of these sentences expresses fear or apprehension?

options.text: What about another cup of tea?
What if the boss stops paying the workers?
What this child needs is a good education.
What's the French word for steering wheel?

questions.explanation: "What if the boss stops paying the workers?" is the one: the frame What if imagines something bad that has not happened yet, and imagining it is what makes it a fear. "What this child needs is a good education." insists on one point, and its what can be replaced by the thing that. "What's the French word for steering wheel?" asks for a piece of information, and "What about another cup of tea?" offers an idea. The classic trap is to sort these sentences by their punctuation: three of them end with a question mark and only one asks for a fact.

questions.prompt: The narrator hears the voice on the telephone and understands that the car behind her is no danger at all. Which word of the lesson names what she feels then?

options.text: relieved
terrified
worried
nervous

questions.explanation: "relieved" is the word: you are relieved when a fear you were carrying turns out to be for nothing, which is precisely the last line of this story. "terrified" is what she was while the car would not overtake, and "nervous" and "worried" both name stages on the way to that fear. All three belong before the telephone call, not after it.
